meta.title: Japanese — JLPT N1
meta.subtitle: 3,055 more words, taking you to about 7,740 — study after N2
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Japanese → English (see the word as it is written, recall its reading and meaning) and English → Japanese. Each word is ONE note with TWO cards, each scheduled on its own. 3055 words for JLPT N1, the fifth and last level of the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test (the board's own summary: "The ability to understand Japanese used in a variety of circumstances."), taking you to about 7,740 words in all. — THE LIST IS UNOFFICIAL, and that has to be said first: the JLPT has published no vocabulary list since its 2010 revision — its FAQ says a list "was not necessarily appropriate" — so every JLPT word list is someone's compilation. This one is the most widely used, Jonathan Waller's, built from the pre-2010 test specifications and mapped onto the five levels; words from it do turn up a level higher or lower in the real test. 347 of the list's rows for this level are words already carded at a lower level and are not carded twice. 14 rows have no entry in JMdict (single-character prefixes such as 依、於、仮) and are left out rather than glossed from nowhere. — The front shows the word as a Japanese reader writes it: kanji, or kana where the dictionary marks the word as usually written in kana (193 of these). The back puts the reading over the kanji as furigana and the Hepburn romaji beneath it, spelled from the kana (so おう is "ou", not "ō": kana alone cannot say whether it is one long vowel or two; katakana's ー is a macron; a particle は is "wa"), then the meanings, one row per kanji with its meanings, on and kun readings and the parts it is drawn from, the words of the lists built on a single kanji, and a fold of real sentences. 2693 of the 3055 words carry example sentences, up to three apiece; Tatoeba has nothing usable for the other 362, which are kept because a word is on the list for being worth knowing, with the word picked out in colour, furigana over the kanji, and a speaker beside each. — Word list: Jonathan Waller's JLPT lists (tanos.co.uk, CC BY), as joined to JMdict by stephenmk/yomitan-jlpt-vocab (CC BY-SA 4.0). Readings, meanings, parts of speech and the "usually written in kana" marks: JMdict (Electronic Dictionary Research and Development Group, CC BY-SA 4.0). Furigana on the headword: JmdictFurigana (CC BY-SA 4.0). Kanji meanings and readings: KANJIDIC2 (EDRDG, CC BY-SA 4.0). The parts each kanji is drawn from: KanjiVG (Ulrich Apel, CC BY-SA 3.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR; the readings over them and the frequency order come from segmenting that corpus with MeCab and the UniDic dictionary, so a reading over an example sentence is a machine's and can occasionally be wrong — the headword's own reading is the dictionary's.
